course_details.Overview of class: AY26-27. This course introduces students to an overview of the history of late Wartime and Post War Japan until the present day, while introducing them to various historical methodological approaches to Japanese history. The course is organized into three parts following the shifting forms of power Japan has wielded on the world stage. The first part deals with Japan's ultimate decline as an expansionist Imperial Power, detailing the final years of WWII and defeat by the U.S. and allied forces, as well as the subsequent occupation. The second part of the course details Japan's rise to economic power from the 1950s to the 1980s, covering the Americanization of Japanese culture, the dramatic shift in domestic living standards, the increasing dominance of Japanese export goods, and the build up of the asset price bubble in the 1980s. The third part of the course details the fall of Japan as an economic power following the bursting of the asset bubble in the 1990s and the rise of Japan as a cultural power in the early 21st century. Students will learn that while Japanese economic power on the world stage waned its cultural cache grew as it exported anime, food, clothing styles and more, burnished by the "Cool Japan Policy." Students will, in each part of the course, engage with Japanese history through primary sources including political documents, literature, movies, anime and manga, and more as well as supporting secondary source readings. Ultimately students will come to understand the past 80 years of Japanese history as well as the tools historians use to analyze it.
course_details.Learning Objectives:
Students will learn the past 80 years of Japanese history.
Students will engage with a variety of primary sources from post war Japan
Students will become familiar with various historical methodologies used to understand Postwar Japan and its primary sources.
Students will learn and practice historical analysis, writing, and argumentation.

instructors: Introduction to Japanese Film, Media, and Visual Culture

course_details.Overview of class: AY26-27. This course offers a history of Japanese cinema from its earliest days through the so-called "Golden Age" of the 1950s. We will consider how film, animation, and other moving image technologies have reflected historical moments and shaped cultural discourses in modern Japan. Focusing on films that raise disciplinary questions related to the cinematic medium, Japan, and history, we will examine, among other topics, the era of silent cinema; the relationship between nationhood and the formation of a "national" cinema; technological transformations and the coming of sound; the wartime period; cinema during the occupation; and 1950s modernism. This overview will engage with several genres, from avant garde, to middle class movies, melodrama, period pieces, kaijū and others. We will also study the place of important individual directors - Ozu, Mizoguchi, and Kurosawa - within the broader economic and institutional contexts of Japanese cinema and its global circulation. Students will learn how to critically analyze the filmic medium from multiple theoretical perspectives while gaining an understanding of the major figures and movements in the history of Japanese cinema.
course_details.Learning Objectives:
How to critically analyze the filmic medium from multiple theoretical perspectives
To identify the major figures and movements of Japanese cinema.
How to interpret Japanese films as products of and commentary on particular moments in Japanese and global history.

course_details.Overview of class:
AY26-27. In an era when global migration and diasporic ways of life have become more commonplace than ever, how do we understand questions of Korean culture and identity? This course approaches this question through a historical inquiry into the discursive construction of Korean national subjectivity and its political, social, and cultural consequences. Beginning with the Chosŏn dynasty's encounter with the modern world system of nation-states in the nineteenth century, the course equips students with critical frameworks for exploring modern Korean culture and art. The term culture in the course title is broadly defined, encompassing not only works of art and cultural texts but also systems of thought and social practices developed throughout modern Korean history.

The course explores a broad range of questions: What is Korean literature, and how is it tied to the modern theorization and understanding of literature (munhak)? What do we make of the fact that the very notion of autonomous art and culture is a modern construction? What is national cinema, and what roles do literature, film, and art play in the construction of national subjectivity and identity? How have Korean writers and artists navigated the complex and ongoing process of identity formation amid the tumultuous histories of colonialism, national division, diasporic displacement, and authoritarian rule? While encouraging students to question assumptions about a homogeneous nation or national culture with an unchanging, seemingly "natural" essence, the course situates Korean art and culture within the broader history of modern Korea.
course_details.Learning Objectives:
By the end of the class, students are expected to:
1. Grasp the historicity of cultural and epistemological concepts, including national culture.
2. Comprehend the intimate relationship between art, culture, identity formation, and political consciousness.
3. Historically situate canonical examples of modern Korean literature and films, recognizing their pivotal role in the development of national consciousness.
4. Analyze individual Korean artworks within the context of the artistic and cultural movements of each historical period, delving into their deeper social, ideological, and political connotations.
5. Comprehensively understand the modern history of Korea with a particular emphasis on the political and cultural history of South Korea, while acknowledging its interconnectedness with various diasporic Korean identities and cultures.
course_details.Teaching Method: • Discussion complemented with lectures. Students are required to participate actively in class discussions and in-class activities. Active participation necessitates completing all assigned readings before coming to class and being prepared to contribute to a lively and informed class discussion.
course_details.Evaluation Method: Grades will largely be determined by student comprehension of lectures and readings, discussion, and a combination of smaller and in-depth writing assignments.

course_details.Overview of class: AY 26 -27. This class will examine how the 1947 partition of India has been engaged in literature and popular culture, moving from contemporary depictions from the 1940s to its continued invocation in India, Pakistan and Bangladesh today. We will read/watch these texts alongside the extensive body of scholarship on Partition from History, Anthropology and Gender Studies with particular attention to the historiography of Partition and South Asian nationalisms. Throughout, we will engage with the idea of Partition as an "event" and ask how Partition continues to inflect life in South Asia and beyond today.

course_details.Overview of class: AY 26-27 India is home to the second largest population of Muslims on earth (slightly outnumbering both of its neighbors, Pakistan and Bangladesh). It's also host to the world's largest film industry, best known as Bollywood, in which Muslims have historically played an outsized role. Little wonder, then, that Bollywood films regularly feature Muslim characters, social spaces, and cultural references that are readily marked or coded as "Islamic." But in spite of a large coterie of Muslims working within the industry - as actors, song writers, or producers - the representation of Muslims in Indian films has consistently raised complex issues around ideas of identity and belonging in a nation where they constitute a clear and conspicuous minority. We will read these films against the historical backdrop of the search for national identity and inclusivity in post-colonial India. Students will be given the opportunity not only to learn about Indian (particularly Bombay) cinema, but also to explore how cinematic representations intersect with issues of identity and belonging in the modern nation-state.

course_details.Overview of class: AY26-27. What are the distinctive features of Tibetan literature? In what ways has Buddhism shaped Tibetan literary genres? How have various forms of Tibetan literature developed over more than a millennium? This course introduces students to Tibet's rich literary traditions through English translations from the imperial period through the early nineteenth century. Students will explore diverse genres including spiritual biography, treasure texts, poetry, historical chronicles, philosophical treatises, and folk literature, examining how Buddhist philosophy and practice have profoundly influenced narrative structures, poetic conventions, and literary production. Through close reading of primary texts alongside secondary scholarship, students will analyze the deep intertwinement of religious concerns and literary expression across Tibetan history. No prior knowledge of Tibetan language, Buddhism, or Tibetan history is required. Students will develop critical reading and analytical writing skills while gaining appreciation for a literary tradition that bridges spiritual quest and human experience, oral and written forms, and religious and secular themes.This course is open to all with no prerequisites and no knowledge of Tibetan language and literature is required.
course_details.Learning Objectives:
1. Identify and describe major themes in Tibetan literary expression
2. Recognize distinctive features of Tibetan literary genres and storytelling conventions
3. Understand basic concepts of Tibetan Buddhism as they appear in literary contexts
4. Contextualize Tibetan literature within its historical and cultural settings
5. Analyze the role of translation in shaping readers' access to Tibetan literature

course_details.Overview of class: AY 26-27. This course explores the birth and development of Tibetan literature beginning in the 1950s when Tibet became part of the newly established People's Republic of China, with a focus on its booming in the 1980s, in the wake of the new economic and political reforms. Although Tibet was a civilization uniquely characterized by a religious literature produced and consumed in monastic institutions, the nature of literature and literacy has changed in Tibet in the past seventy years, becoming more accessible to the wider public. Tibetan writers have used fiction and poetry in new ways to reflect on life, rapidly changing worldviews, and critiques of the past as well as the present. This course will introduce students to a number of modern and contemporary Tibetan literary works, mostly secular in nature, including short novels, fiction, and poetry in English translation, as well as academic studies and scholarly analysis of modern Tibetan literature.
course_details.Learning Objectives:
1. Analyze Themes of Identity, Displacement, and Cultural Change in Contemporary Tibetan Literature
2. Compare Literary Responses to Distinct Political and Social Contexts
3. Recognize Genre Innovation and Experimentation in Contemporary Tibetan Writing
4. Understand the Multilingual Dimensions of Contemporary Tibetan Literature
5. Contextualize Contemporary Tibetan Literature Within Recent Historical Events

course_details.Overview of class:
AY26-27. In 1983, Edward Feigenbaum, a renowned computer scientist at Stanford, and journalist Pamela McCorduck warned that Japan's Fifth Generation Computer project posed a challenge to American technological leadership and perhaps to the future of artificial intelligence itself. A few years later, Japan studies scholar and linguist Marshall J. Unger called much of this vision a "fifth generation fallacy," arguing that Japan's heavy investment in AI was inseparable from the distinctive challenges that East Asian writing systems posed in digital environments, as well as from the retraining of its population in preparation for the information age. This course begins from that geopolitical tension and its historicity: today's AI discourse has a long genealogy that reveals the social, political, and cultural nature of technology and media infrastructure. AI has never been only about whether machines can think. With its very definition and underlying assumptions, including what exactly counts as intelligence, changing across different times and places, its longer global history opens up space for critical inquiry into how culture, politics, and different forms of body politics are constitutive of technologies.
Today's artificial intelligence—more specifically, the large language models that have come to dominate public discussion of AI—is often presented as a radically new technology transforming labor, writing, and everyday life. With its focus on the twentieth- and twenty-first-century history of global technoscientific modernity, this course encourages students to take a historicizing view. Rather than beginning with contemporary AI systems, it places them within longer histories of cybernetics, automation, writing, and computation, with particular, though not exclusive, attention to East Asia. Drawing on plural, global histories of AI, cybernetics, and media technologies that resist technological determinism, the course is designed to help students develop critical literacy through readings in critical media studies, science and technology studies, the history of science and technology, and East Asian studies.
